books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Treaty of December 30, 1853 (Gadsden Purchase), Article I, as ratified; Article III as ratified set the payment at $10 million. Public domain.
stimulus.text:
Article I. The Mexican Republic agrees to designate the following as her true limits with the United States for the future: . . . Beginning in the Gulf of Mexico, three leagues from land, opposite the mouth of the Rio Grande, as provided in the 5th article of the treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo; thence, as defined in the said article, up the middle of that river to the point where the parallel of 31° 47′ north latitude crosses the same; thence due west one hundred miles; thence south to the parallel of 31° 20′ north latitude; thence along the said parallel of 31° 20′ to the 111th meridian of longitude west of Greenwich; thence in a straight line to a point on the Colorado River twenty English miles below the junction of the Gila and Colorado rivers . . .

[Article III, as ratified, set the payment to Mexico at $10 million.]

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The United States sought the land described in Article I mainly because it wanted which of the following?

options.text: A port on the Gulf of California for the whaling fleet.
options.misconception: Whaling played no part in the purchase; the land was wanted for a railroad route.

options.text: Farmland for the freedpeople who would leave the South after emancipation.
options.misconception: Emancipation came a decade later, and the purchase was about a railroad, not resettlement.

options.text: A southern route for a transcontinental railroad to the Pacific.
A buffer against a British invasion from Canada.
options.misconception: The land lay on the Mexican border, far from Canada, and Britain was not threatening an invasion.

rationales.A: No whaling port was at stake; the purchase was about getting a railroad across the southern desert.
rationales.B: Emancipation was a decade away; the purchase was made for a railroad route, not for resettlement.
rationales.C: The strip south of the Gila offered flat ground for a southern transcontinental railroad, which the northern routes could not match.
rationales.D: The land bordered Mexico, not Canada, and Britain threatened no invasion from the north.
rationales.general:
1. Look at the shape of the land in Article I: a strip running west from the Rio Grande to the Colorado.
2. Ask what that strip is good for. It is low, flat desert — the easiest ground for rails to the Pacific.
3. That was the point. The United States bought the strip to carry a southern railroad to California.
Remember: a land deal's shape often gives away its purpose — a long thin strip is a route, not a farm.
